title: How many times do we keep each shared prime?
description: The numbers two hundred twenty five and seven hundred fifty are written as products of primes, and the shared primes are kept the smaller number of times each. Keeko doubts this and wants to keep five three times, which would give a number larger than two hundred twenty five.
teaching_notes: One idea: a shared prime is kept only as many times as the number that holds it fewer times. Watch for students who keep a prime as many times as the bigger number has it and get a number that cannot divide the smaller one.

video_script.why: The child has found the highest common factor of two numbers with one shared prime count each and now meets a prime that is shared with different counts.
video_script.substitution: Write both numbers as products of primes, keep each shared prime the smaller number of times, and multiply.
video_script.anchor: The prime products of 225 and 750 written one under the other, as in the book's example, with the shared primes lit.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko keeps five three times because 750 has three fives, and gets three hundred seventy five, which is larger than 225 and so cannot divide it.
video_script.payoff_line: The highest common factor is seventy five
never_show: 375 as the highest common factor, marked right
maths_rules: common primes are 3 and 5; 2 is not in 225
3 appears twice in 225 and once in 750, the smaller count is 1
5 appears twice in 225 and three times in 750, the smaller count is 2
slip: 3 × 5 × 5 × 5 = 375, which is larger than 225 so cannot divide 225
video_script.design: One idea: keep the smaller count of each shared prime, here with two different shared primes. Assumes the child can write a number as a product of primes. The prime products stay on the board from step one to the answer.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We must find the highest common factor of two hundred twenty five and seven hundred fifty.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Both can be written as products of primes. Which primes do they share, and how many times?

beats.on_screen: the two numbers stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a number holding two 5s and a number holding three 5s; 5 × 5 = 25 fits inside both; a third 5 fits only in the bigger one

marks.m1: two cards appear, one holding two 5s and one holding three 5s
marks.m3: the third 5 on the bigger card is shown with nothing to match it on the smaller card

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Picture one number holding two fives and another holding three fives.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two fives fit inside both of them.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The third five has nothing to match in the smaller number, so it cannot be shared.

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, the two numbers two hundred twenty five and seven hundred fifty.

beats.on_screen: To find: the HCF of 225 and 750

marks.m1: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find their highest common factor.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: write each number as a product of primes: 225 = 3 × 3 × 5 × 5; 750 = 2 × 3 × 5 × 5 × 5

marks.m1: the words product of primes are written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, write each number as a product of primes.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two hundred twenty five is three times three times five times five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Seven hundred fifty is two times three times five times five times five.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: primes found in both products: 3 and 5; 2 is not in 225

marks.m1: the threes and the fives are lit in both products
marks.m2: the 2 in 750 is crossed with a note not in 225

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, pick the primes that appear in both products.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>These are three and five, because two is not in two hundred twenty five.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: keep each common prime the smaller number of times: 3 is twice in 225 and once in 750, keep one 3; 5 is twice in 225 and three times in 750, keep two 5s

marks.m1: the words smaller number of times are written
marks.m2: the counts of 3 are written, twice and once, and one 3 is kept
marks.m3: the counts of 5 are written, twice and three times, and two 5s are kept

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, keep each common prime the smallest number of times it appears.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two hundred twenty five has two threes and seven hundred fifty has one, so keep one three.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Two hundred twenty five has two fives and seven hundred fifty has three, so keep two fives.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: multiply the kept primes: HCF = 3 × 5 × 5

marks.m1: the kept 3 and the two 5s slide together and HCF = 3 × 5 × 5 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, multiply the primes we kept, one three and two fives.

marks.m1: the answer is written and boxed
marks.m2: the kept primes are lit in both products

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The highest common factor is seventy five.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Dividing two hundred twenty five by it gives three, and dividing seven hundred fifty gives ten.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the two prime products
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 3 × 5 × 5 × 5 = 375, struck out because 375 is larger than 225; the answer 75 is lit again

marks.m3: 375 is set beside 225 and the bubble is struck out
marks.m4: the two 5s are lit again and the answer 75 returns

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks we should take five three times, because seven hundred fifty has three fives.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That gives three times five times five times five, which is three hundred seventy five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>But three hundred seventy five is bigger than two hundred twenty five. It cannot be a factor of the smaller number.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>A shared prime can be kept only as many times as the smaller number holds it. Two fives stay, and the answer is seventy five.
